extracted.intended_audience: logicians, philosophers, and scientific authors concerned with designing precise terminology and philosophical language
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and using a philosophical/scientific vocabulary: ensuring terms have precise meanings, providing descriptive terminology for observation, and managing changes in word-connotation over time. Emphasizes conventions, perceptual grounding of technical terms, and exemplary practices from botany and mineralogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each term must convey a determinate and unmistakable meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: That its terms shall each of them convey a determinate and unmistakable meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fundamental requisite of a language fitted for investigating truth; terms used in scientific/philosophical discourse should have fixed, clear meanings so they reliably convey the intended concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: No important meaning without an appropriated word
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no important meaning without its word. Whatever we have occasion to think of often, and for scientific purposes, ought to have a name appropriated to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For effective record and communication, frequently considered concepts must be named; absence of a name hinders precise recording of observations and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate Descriptive Terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be all such names, as are needful for making such a record of individual observations that the words of the record shall exactly show what fact it is which has been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive terminology must allow records to show exactly what was observed. This includes names for elementary sensations and for commonly recurring combinations to promote clarity and brevity in descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical terms fixed by convention and taught through perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of [descriptive] technical terms can be fixed in the first instance only by convention, and can be made intelligible only by presenting to the senses that which the terms are to signify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical/descriptive terms (e.g. color names like 'apple-green' or 'French gray') must be associated immediately with the perception they denote rather than left to vague common-language suggestions; convention and perceptual exemplars fix meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary sensations cannot be defined; must be learned experientially
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of elementary sensations, or elementary feelings of any sort, can not be defined; nor is there any mode of making their signification known but by making the learner experience the sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only by presenting the sensation or referring to a remembered perception can the meaning be taught — definitions do not suffice for elementary sensory terms. Thus precise training/illustration is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give distinctive names to frequent combinations to aid brevity and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity of description, and clearness (which often depends very much on brevity), are greatly promoted by giving distinctive names not to the elements alone, but also to all combinations which are of frequent recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create fixed names for recurring compound phenomena (e.g. botanical compound terms); this reduces circumlocution and increases clarity in scientific writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and fix specialized nomenclature (botany/mineralogy examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation of an exact and extensive descriptive language for botany has been executed with a degree of skill and felicity... every part of a plant has been named; and the form of every part, even the most minute, has had a large assemblage of descriptive terms appropriated to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the botanical/mineralogical practice as a model: fix terms consistently (Linnaean reform), introduce terms for important distinctions (calyx, corolla, stamens, pistils), and adopt classified color scales and hardness scales (Werner, Mohs) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numerical measures for properties when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Some properties, as specific gravity, by their definition give at once a numerical measure; and others, as crystalline form, require a very considerable array of mathematical calculation and reasoning, to point out their relations and gradations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, express properties numerically (e.g. specific gravity, Mohs hardness) to increase precision and comparability across observations and reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid corruptions, vulgarisms and mistranslations that generalize or distort meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulgarisms, which creep in nobody knows how, are daily depriving the English language of valuable modes of expressing thought... Examples: 'transpire' used for 'to happen', 'aggravating' for 'provoking', misuse of 'alone' as an adverb, 'predicate' for 'predict', and translators' false equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such corruptions narrow expressive resources and force circumlocutions. Authors and editors should resist fashionable misuses and mistranslations that shift meanings and render technical vocabulary ambiguous or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know a term's history before attempting to alter its use
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever seeks to introduce a more correct use of a term with which important associations are connected, should be required to possess an accurate acquaintance with the history of the particular word, and of the opinions which in different stages of its progress it served to express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proposing semantic changes, investigate prior meanings and the propositions that rested on them; avoid redefining in ways that would render formerly true propositions false without full consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: When meaning is irrevocably changed, define according to the new meaning and retain former sense as secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: The logician... should submit to them with a good grace when they are irrevocably effected, and if a definition is necessary, define the word according to its new meaning; retaining the former as a second signification, if it is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a shift in common usage is permanent, adopt the new meaning in definitions used for current discourse, but preserve previous meanings as subsidiary senses when useful for historical or philosophical clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of connotation leading to question-begging names
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional connotation... of agreeableness or painfulness... gives rise to the fallacy of 'question-begging names.' The very property which we are inquiring whether a thing possesses or not, has become so associated with the name of the thing as to be part of its meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using terms whose connotation presupposes the point under debate (especially in moral/social discourse); recognize affective associations as they can disguise assumptions and bias reasoning.
